chapter: Return to New York, addiction, health and the NBC job
title: Emphysema, smoking since twelve and the 1934 appendix operations
summary: He dates emphysema to 1969 and explains smoking began after a Tulsa operation that shaped his reckless life.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: '69. Trying to make a square dollar. Say work won't hurt you. It killed me. Because after all of these habits that I've had and all of the other things that I've done that was negative to my metabolism, you know, my being, none of them did the damage to me than that job and cigarettes. I let cigarettes knock the pins out from under me.
Is that what the emphysema is attributed to? Cigarette smoking?

A long period of time of smoking, combined with nerves. Nerves goes along with it. You can't have emphysema without being nervous, no, no. And then there's people that get emphysema without smoking, just by being exposed to a lot of smoke, you know, over a period of time. Now, like I started smoking when I was 12 years old. I was sniffing and smoking. Then I had an appendectomy, a ruptured appendectomy, it wasn't ruptured. I'm sorry. It was--my appendix had formed a -- a corruption had formed over my appendix, and they had to operate on me to get this poison out before peritonitis or gangrene or something set in. And I had an alcoholic doctor, family doctor, and he planted his knee in the middle of my spine and pulled my shoulders, and my shoulders was kind of curved

inwardly, you know. I couldn't straighten up, from this appendix thing hurting me so. And when he straightened me up, I fainted right there on the floor. And it started, this thing, to leak, and the Catholics sent me to St. John's Hospital over there in Tulsa, Oklahoma, where they didn't receive any blacks. There was only three blacks there the whole time I was there. One was a basketball player from a little town called Bartlesville. He was a good basketball player, but he got both feet broke. The way the fellows fell on him, the feet was broken in the arches. And another little kid that lived down in Tulsa got his leg broke. He was like a little scavenger. He didn't have any parents. Home was where he made it. He was just raising himself, you know, stealing and everything else. And he got his leg broke somehow. I don't know how he got it broken. Probably jumping off a train or something. And they sent him out there. But other than that, there wasn't no more blacks in this hospital. So the Sister out there, name was Sister Bonneville, she suggested that I chew chewing gum for my nerves. I said, 'No, I don't like chewing gum.' She said, 'Well, why don't you smoke?' I said, 'Well, all right, I'll smoke.' I'm getting the license to smoke, now. I can go home and smoke in front of my parents, you know, or ask them for money for cigarettes. The Sister says, all right, smoke, for my nerves. So now, I've been smoking from, let's see, 12 years old up to 59. Wow. Let's see. It'd be -- I started smoking

in 1930, slipping out smoking. Then '34, New Years Day, they had me on the operating table, in '34. I stayed in the hospital, I guess, about six months. They made this incision, and they inserted a bicycle tube in there, for it to drain out. Well, at that time they didn't have penicillin or any myecin drugs or sulfadrug. They didn't have anything like that. So I'm lucky to be here now, you know, for what they had to work with at that time. And instead of this corruption coming out of this incision, it passed by the incision and formed a pocket on the other side. And it healed down to the size of a nickel, which meant all of the corruption wasn't out. So they made another incision, and this time, instead of it coming out, it went back to its original position. So they cut on me the third time. This time, it healed, and I went back to school. I think I mentioned it on a previous tape. Went back to school and picked up my trumpet too soon and ruptured the incision inwardly, inside, you know, tore the stitches loose. But the years fly so you wonder where the time went, you know. Like from that day on, the doctor telling me that I could die from this or I could live to be a ripe old age, I lived every day from then on like it was the last one. You know? So I was a pretty bad boy from then on, you know? I did everything that come along. I was adventuresome and everything else, you know?
